exp_mews_squad_blurb: Led a cross-functional squad responsible for the user experience across all Mews products. We took over the shells of every product, unifying and standardising them, along with the Dashboard of the main application, the PMS, and parts of the Smart Assistant Search engine. Designed and built the app switcher for the whole Mews ecosystem, end to end. Also took on backend maintenance over assets and translations. Planned the work and mentored junior engineers.
exp_mews_techlead_title: Tech Lead — Mews Design System, Platform team
exp_mews_techlead_blurb: On top of my senior engineer role, I took on the technical lead of the Mews Design System, as formal code owner of its libraries: the legacy library and the new implementations for both B2B and B2C. Among many other initiatives, I was responsible for, and the main contributor to, the work that followed an independent accessibility audit of Mews's guest-facing products against WCAG 2.1 AA and the European Accessibility Act — with the design system as one of its largest areas. Beyond that, I worked on large, key new components such as the DataGrid, built on TanStack Table and taken a long way past it: client-side, server-side and tree variants behind one API, and many user-facing features.
exp_mews_senior_title: Senior Software Engineer — Mews Design System, Platform team
exp_mews_senior_blurb: Shipped component libraries and frontend tooling for a large React/TypeScript monorepo, as the main contributor on my team and one of the top contributors to the whole repository. Likewise one of the main contributors to the multi-brand design-tokens pipeline (Figma → Token Studio → Style Dictionary), where one source of truth drives four themes across two brands on web and Android.
exp_liferay_blurb: Product engineer on the Tango team, working in Java and React through Liferay's portlets. I worked mostly on the Content Dashboard — audit charts, the item info panel, previews, versions, sharing and subscriptions — and on the Frontend Data Set, the tables shared across the platform; besides, prioritised segment variations for Collections, down to the Service Builder layer, and the Page Audit built on Google PageSpeed.
exp_docline_blurb: Led the frontend of a telemedicine platform, taking its Vue codebase to the next level — component reusability, best practices, and large-scale refactors, including introducing an app-wide shared store as the single source of truth for application state. Reviewed architecture, standardised code reviews, fostered a strong team culture, and improved the existing design system across Vue, TS and SCSS.
exp_indra_po_title: Product Owner & Engineer — Onesait platform website
exp_indra_po_blurb: Owned and delivered the main web app promoting Onesait products, bridging engineering and marketing. Led a team of four engineers and one designer, managing multiple stakeholders.
exp_indra_consultant_title: Senior Software Engineer & Consultant — Onesait Design System
exp_indra_consultant_blurb: Main delivery engineer on the Vue.js-based design system, and the go-to reference supporting every product engineering team adopting it.
exp_ironhack_blurb: Taught intensive full-stack web development bootcamps. Fast-paced and hands-on — and nothing hones your own fundamentals quite like teaching them to others.
exp_tau_blurb: Led a team of up to six developers at a design-led agency — client-facing work, pitching, and mentoring juniors — delivering marketing and corporate sites, e-commerce stores, and a steady stream of microsites for clients like Edelvives, ECAM, Universidad Autónoma, Mapfre and Telefónica. In a studio that lived and breathed design, the bar was pixel-perfect: high-craft UI, rich interactions, and truly responsive layouts, on jQuery, Bootstrap, PHP and WordPress, with Less and Sass built on Node, and our first steps in Angular.
exp_aulacm_blurb: Helped build and maintain the company's main site and the client websites delivered by its agency arm — my first taste of agency work and shipping custom WordPress in PHP. Doubled as the in-house WordPress instructor, teaching plugins, themes, styling and the PHP basics that make it all tick — and learning plenty the honest way myself.
exp_prev_blurb: Before software, sound for film and TV, from 2002: location sound, post-production and mixing. Post-production and music recording on En la cuna del aire and sound design on Flores de Ruanda, both Goya winners for Best Documentary Short; location sound and post on About Ndugu, shot in Kenya and premiered at the Berlinale. With my friend Iván I founded lacasaestudio, still going.

ui_cs_code_private: The code is private — happy to walk through it on a call.
cs_billing_intro: A billing engine that repays cash advances by taking a share of a merchant's daily revenue, driven day by day against a live API across a simulated month. It began as a take-home exercise, which is why the source stays private — I'm happy to walk anyone through it.
cs_billing_n1_h: One backlog, not three code paths
cs_billing_n1_b: Revenue that arrives late, a daily charge cap, and a charge the processor rejects look like three problems. They are one: an amount that could not settle today. Each advance carries a backlog, all three feed it, and the next day drains it under the same rules. The hard part of the brief turned out to be small once it had the right name.
cs_billing_n2_b: Amounts arrive as two-decimal strings, parsed once at the edge into a branded integer type and formatted once on the way out. The arithmetic in between goes through helpers that re-validate, so a float can never reach a balance. Rounding happens in exactly one place, and is documented because the spec was silent on it.
cs_billing_n3_h: A port, so every edge case is provable
cs_billing_n3_b: A live API cannot be asked to reject a charge or withhold a day's revenue on demand. One interface with two implementations — the real client and an in-memory fake — turns each failure mode into a deterministic test. All 136 of them run offline, in seconds.
cs_billing_n4_h: Decisions written down where the spec was silent
cs_billing_n4_b: Rounding, the accrual window, what becomes of an advance that cannot repay before the period ends, whether the daily cap is per advance or per mandate: each chosen once, pinned by a test, and listed with its reasoning. An architecture decision record covers the alternatives rejected — including the monorepo that would have demonstrated more and proved less.
cs_billing_shot1_alt: The run report: outstanding portfolio balance, collection statistics and every advance in the run.
cs_billing_shot1_cap: Each run writes a self-contained HTML report — no server, no build step, opens from disk.
cs_billing_shot2_alt: One advance's event ledger, showing eight consecutive rejected charges.
cs_billing_shot2_cap: An advance whose mandate stopped working. The balance stays intact and a human gets told; “stalled” is a reporting diagnosis, never a state the domain invents.
proj_billing_desc: A daily billing engine for cash advances: a pure domain core behind a ports-and-adapters seam, with late revenue, daily caps and rejected charges all carried forward by one mechanism.
map_pick_b: Each one says what it is, what it does and why it is there.
proj_perico_desc: Rewrites plain Spanish in the voice of a cycling commentator — a RAG pipeline in Python, with FastAPI, pgvector and Claude.
proj_review_desc: An AI-assisted grader for university assignments: Claude grades a batch of submissions against the rubric, quoting the work for every deduction, and the teacher validates each grade in a viewer.
proj_lacasaestudio_desc: The website of a recording project at a residential studio in Granada, moved from WordPress to Astro and Supabase, with an admin the studio runs itself and a Telegram chat where it asks for changes that an AI agent makes in the repo.
cs_ensayadero_tagline: A rehearsal room that listens back.
cs_ensayadero_intro: A rehearsal tool for bands: upload a recording and get it back split into stems, with MIDI and an editable chord chart, in a multi-track mixer. In invite-only beta.
cs_ensayadero_n1_h: Self-hosted audio ML, no paid APIs
cs_ensayadero_n1_b: A Python pipeline — Demucs for stem separation, Basic Pitch and Omnizart for transcription, Omnizart and madmom for chords — runs on TensorFlow and PyTorch, which is why it ships in the same Docker image as the Next.js server, self-hosted with Coolify, behind a job queue that recovers interrupted work on restart.
cs_ensayadero_n2_b: Next.js 16 and React 19 with RLS-aware API routes; Supabase for Postgres, Google OAuth with an allow-list and role claims, and Storage for stems, MIDI and charts. Playback in the browser with Tone.js and wavesurfer.
cs_perico_tagline: A translator with a very specific voice.
cs_perico_intro: Paste ordinary Spanish and it comes back in the voice of Perico Delgado, the Tour winner turned cycling commentator. Live at radioperico.com, with a public course on how it was built.
cs_perico_n1_h: RAG over a corpus of his own words
cs_perico_n1_b: A corpus built from transcribed broadcasts and classified with an LLM, embedded with a multilingual sentence-transformers model and indexed in pgvector on Supabase. Each request retrieves the closest phrases and hands them, as examples to follow, to the Claude API — with the right model for each use case.
cs_perico_n2_b: Python and FastAPI serve the translation as a stream, with embeddings from that same model, now on my own server, and pooled connections to Postgres; React and Vite on the front, with dictation and speech synthesis. An evaluation suite and spending caps keep it honest.
cs_paellalab_tagline: The arithmetic behind a good rice.
cs_paellalab_intro: Rice and cooking time in; broth, fat, salt and portions out, from how much water each pan actually loses to evaporation. Around the calculator: recipes, a registry of your own pans, a timer and an AI cooking assistant on Llama 3.3. Installable, offline-capable, bilingual.
cs_paellalab_n1_h: A small assistant on cheap inference
cs_paellalab_n1_b: Embeddings from Hugging Face, vector search in Postgres, generation with Llama 3.3 70B on Groq, with rate limiting written into the route itself — a hundred messages a day, ten a minute — sized for roughly fifteen users. A frontier model would have cost more per month than the app is worth, and would not have answered a question about rice any better.
cs_paellalab_n2_b: Only authentication and navigation load eagerly; every landing section waits until it is visible. The gated content exists twice on purpose — enforced on the server, softened on the client with a fade — because the first is the rule and the second is the manners.
cs_paellalab_n3_b: Every pan loses water at its own pace, so each one gets a quick evaporation test. The app turns that measurement into how much broth a given amount of rice needs for the time it will cook, and works out the rest of the quantities from there.
cs_tablux_tagline: From the bin to running the house.
cs_tablux_intro: A HiPOS point-of-sale terminal was about to be thrown away. I took it apart, brought it back to life on Linux and hung it on the wall. From there it grew into one app for every screen at home: the wall, old tablets and our phones. Lights, blinds, plugs, the projector and routines, music, the family agenda, the week's menu and the shopping list — by touch, by voice or with a couple of claps.
cs_tablux_n1_h: My own Linux on an undocumented board
cs_tablux_n1_b: It ran a locked, outdated Android 10 on a Rockchip RK3288 board with no public documentation. After a full backup of the factory system, I wrote the device tree from the vendor's own, built U-Boot with the memory init this board needs, and compiled Linux 6.18 on Armbian with the display drivers it lacked. Screen, touch, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and sound came back one by one — the touch only once I found the GPIO that powers it. Phosh on top turns it into a system made for fingers.
cs_tablux_n2_h: One app, every screen at home
cs_tablux_n2_b: With the wall working, it made more sense as an app for the whole household than as a single screen. Tablux is a PWA, so the same app runs on the wall, on an iPhone, on a 2014 tablet and on a 2020 Android phone. Layout follows each screen's size and behaviour follows its role: shared screens rest at night, with the clock and any running timer, and ask who is using them; personal phones don't. A change made anywhere — on another screen, by a routine, on the device itself — shows on every screen within about two seconds.
cs_tablux_n3_h: The house, over the local network
cs_tablux_n3_b: The wall talks to plugs, bulbs, blinds and the projector over the local network, never through their makers' clouds. Routines like «Modo cine» or «Buenas noches» run on the wall itself — at a set time, by the sun or with two or three claps — so they keep working without internet. «Encender durante» leaves a light or a plug on for a while, and the device switches itself off. No port is open to the outside: the cloud reaches the wall only over Tailscale.
cs_tablux_n4_b: The family agenda comes from Google Calendar. The week's menu draws on a shared recipe book — recipes typed, dictated or brought in from any website — and the shopping list suggests whatever a planned dish still needs. Timers ring on the screen they were set on, with a push notification on the phone. The wall is a Spotify Connect speaker in its own right, and it wakes the house's Cast speakers to play on them too.
cs_tablux_n5_b: Whisper on Groq transcribes and Claude Haiku answers with the same tools the app has — lights, blinds, the projector, routines, menus, agenda, timers, music — then says it out loud. With several screens listening, only the one that heard it best answers. In the chat you can type, talk or send a photo. The same tools make Tablux an MCP server, so any assistant can run the house with a personal key.
cs_tablux_n6_h: A voice and a wake word of its own
cs_tablux_n6_b: The assistant speaks in a voice of its own, which I trained with Voicebox and Runpod: a Piper voice served from my own server, with the wall's own Piper as an offline fallback. The wake word is a model of my own too, trained on Runpod and detected on the device itself — a sidecar on the wall, a WASM engine in the tablets' browsers.
cs_tablux_n7_b: «Abre una PR que…» turns a spoken request into a GitHub issue; Claude Code picks it up in GitHub Actions and opens the pull request, and nothing merges without a tap on a phone.

cs_infrastructure_tagline: Every backend on a server of my own.
cs_infrastructure_intro: Where the backends of my apps live: one ARM VPS running Coolify, with a self-hosted Supabase for each app, an embeddings service, backups in three places and uptime monitoring. This is how it stands in November 2026.
cs_infrastructure_n1_h: One server, not a managed project per app
cs_infrastructure_n1_b: Each app used to have its own managed project on Supabase Cloud, and every new app added another. Now they share one server, each with a Supabase of its own: cheaper by design, and a new app is just one more instance on the same machine. Supabase stayed because every app already spoke supabase-js, so none of them had to change; Appwrite, PocketBase or a stack of my own would have meant rewriting them.
cs_infrastructure_n2_b: Each app gets its own instance, so one app's users and tokens are never valid in another. Each instance runs only the services its app uses, and Kong on a single worker went from 471 MB to 84 MB, which leaves the server plenty of room to grow.
cs_infrastructure_n3_b: The apps that lived on Supabase Cloud moved over changing only the URL and keys, with data, users and files checked against the original before each old project was deleted. The ESP32 devices switched over the air, with a firmware update. One app also left Railway, and now builds and runs as a container on the same server.
cs_infrastructure_n4_b: When Hugging Face's hosted inference stopped answering, one of my apps stopped translating. The same model now runs on the server with ONNX Runtime, in about 400 MB of memory: identical vectors, so nothing in the corpus had to be recomputed.
cs_infrastructure_n5_h: Closed to the outside, copied three times
cs_infrastructure_n5_b: Administration only over Tailscale; only the apps face the internet. Backups in three places: nightly database dumps and files to Backblaze B2, the VPS provider's backups of the whole server, and a Raspberry Pi at home that pulls everything with a read-only key into an encrypted copy on a NAS, out of reach of anyone who gets into the server. The Pi also keeps a mirror of every GitHub repo. Restores tested. Uptime monitoring alerts my phone.
cs_infrastructure_n6_h: Written down as it was built
cs_infrastructure_n6_b: Every decision, keeping the frontends on Vercel among them, is recorded with its date, its reason and the alternatives ruled out, alongside runbooks for migrating an app or restoring a backup.
cs_carabanchel_tagline: A neighbourhood, mapped by the people living in it.
cs_carabanchel_intro: An interactive map of the cultural and commercial fabric of Carabanchel, in Madrid, built with the IED: editors publish collections through a CMS and the public app draws them as layers over Mapbox — local commerce, the people who sustain it, and the places at risk of disappearing. Built by two, not solo.
cs_carabanchel_n1_b: Rather than storing loose latitude and longitude columns, a feature's geometry is a dynamic zone built from GeoJSON components. A non-technical editor fills in a form and the API emits a valid FeatureCollection the map consumes directly — plus bulk import for the collections that arrived as files, and regeneration on save.
cs_carabanchel_n2_h: A composed map, and lists that stay smooth
cs_carabanchel_n2_b: Mapbox GL runs under Leaflet rather than standalone, which kept the plugin ecosystem available, and the side panel virtualises its feature list so a collection of hundreds of points scrolls without dropping frames on the phones people actually walk around with.
cs_meteo_tagline: Our own weather, minute by minute.
cs_meteo_intro: Home weather stations, one or several. An ESP32 on a mast measures temperature, humidity, pressure, wind speed and gusts, wind direction and rain, and sends a reading every minute to a self-hosted Supabase. Every station runs the same firmware with its own identity and key, and a new one joins by following a step-by-step guide. The public dashboard lists the public stations, with a picker when there is more than one, and shows each one's weather live, in charts and beside the forecast; it can also send a notification each morning with the day ahead.
cs_meteo_n1_h: C++ firmware, tested off the board
cs_meteo_n1_b: C++ on the Arduino framework, built with PlatformIO. Interrupts count the anemometer and the rain gauge, each with its own debounce; the gust is the strongest three-second average of the minute, the wind direction a circular mean. Readings wait in memory while the WiFi is down and go out in batches, WiFi and the station's key are set from a phone, and the pure logic is unit-tested on the computer.
cs_meteo_n2_h: A minute at a time, into Postgres
cs_meteo_n2_b: An Edge Function takes each batch with the station's own key, of which only a hash is stored, and a repeated upload never duplicates a minute. Postgres rolls the readings into hourly and daily aggregates with pg_cron, and Vercel Functions serve them as a cached read API, ready for more than one station.
cs_meteo_n3_h: Updates over the air, with a way back
cs_meteo_n3_b: Firmware is published from the command line and assigned station by station. The board checks its size and SHA-256, reboots into it and keeps it only once an upload gets through; if none does within ten minutes, it rolls back and never installs that version again. Stations report their health and events with every upload, readable from anywhere. When noise on the rain gauge turned into phantom downpours one rainy morning, the fix reached the mast that afternoon, without opening the box.
cs_meteo_n4_h: A dashboard, and the forecast at nine
cs_meteo_n4_b: React 19 and Vite, with ECharts and TanStack Query. Current conditions with feels-like temperature; charts for the last 24 hours, the week, a month or any range; wind with its gusts and direction; and the Open-Meteo forecast. Installed as an app, it sends a notification at 9:00 with the day's forecast, its high and low corrected with the station's own readings, triggered by pg_cron and never more than once a day.
cs_meteo_shot1_alt: The station view: today's sky, the last reading, and current temperature, humidity, pressure, wind, gust and rain.
cs_meteo_shot1_cap: Each station's conditions, live, with a reading every minute.
cs_meteo_shot2_alt: The last 24 hours in charts: temperature, humidity, rain, wind with its gusts and direction, pressure and dew point.
cs_meteo_shot2_cap: One chart per measure, over any range from two hours to a custom span.
cs_meteo_shot3_alt: The forecast tab: the coming week day by day, with the chance of rain and the gusts, and the next 24 hours in three-hour steps.
cs_meteo_shot3_cap: The Open-Meteo forecast for the week, in the same app.
cs_canallum_tagline: A house to walk through before it's built.
cs_canallum_intro: Ca Na Llum is a house still on paper, shown on the plot where it will stand: house, garden, natural pool and grove, at any hour of a July day. Orbit it from outside, cut it open as a plan or walk through it room by room, with a mouse, a keyboard or two thumbs on a phone. Or let the guided tour take you through it, by day or by night.
cs_canallum_n1_h: The real plot, from open data
cs_canallum_n1_b: Parcel, terrain and aerial photo come from the land registry and the national mapping agency: the model sits on the real ground with the mountains on the skyline, and trees grow where the photo shows crowns — almonds, figs, olives, carobs and pines. The sun keeps the real latitude and puts the house in the mountain's shade before sunset, and an optional soundscape of cicadas, crickets, an owl and sheep bells follows the hour, all synthesised in the browser.
cs_canallum_n2_h: Quick to open, smooth to walk
cs_canallum_n2_b: Every download starts from the HTML in parallel, height grids travel as prediction residuals and every shader variant compiles before the first frame, so changing the hour or the view, or the lamps coming on at dusk, never stutters. A ?perf=1 panel times each pass on the GPU and the CPU. Measured with it, trees went to three levels of detail, the sun's shadow redraws at 30 Hz and the resolution follows the frame time against the screen's refresh rate. Phones get lighter settings.
cs_canallum_n3_b: Seven taps on the pool start a night party: festoons, dancing mannequins, a DJ, an inflatable flamingo adrift and a house track synthesised live, until the lights go out one by one. A poster in one bedroom turns the place into a dark, overgrown double of itself: a red-black sky with lightning, spores drifting indoors, veined vines up the walls, creatures modelled and rigged in code, and something enormous moving behind the mountains.
cs_canallum_n4_b: The furniture is modelled in Blender from Python: beds, sofas, an oak rush-seat chair, the bathrooms, linen curtains, framed pictures, the things on the kitchen island. One command exports the house and bakes its indirect light with Cycles at five hours of a July day and a lamp-lit night, plus a roofless one for the plan, each denoised with OIDN. The model blends them by the sun's position. Every piece is hash-checked against the bake, and anything changed since falls back to live light.
cs_canallum_shot1_alt: A bird's-eye view of the house in the 3D model: the tiled roof, the natural pool, the vegetable garden and the grove on real terrain, with the side panel for views, light and layers.
cs_canallum_shot1_cap: The house on its real plot and terrain, both taken from open data.
cs_canallum_shot2_alt: Plan view with the roof off: each room labelled with its name and floor area, with the furniture in place.
cs_canallum_shot2_cap: The plan, with the rooms and their floor area.
cs_canallum_shot3_alt: The house at night: lights on inside, stars and the outline of the mountains.
cs_canallum_shot3_cap: The light follows the hour of a July day, night included.
cs_canallum_shot4_cap: The guided tour: one take through every room and round the garden.
cs_canallum_shot4_alt: The guided tour in the living room: the dining table, the kitchen island under its hood and the sofa beneath the timber roof, with the caption card on the left.
cs_canallum_n6_b: Five minutes through every room, west to east, and round the garden, worked out in advance: the camera always looks where it walks, slows down at each place, turns to it with a caption and moves on. Tests walk the whole route against the walls and furniture, capping its speed and its turns, and another walks the whole floor from the hall and fails on any corner you could get stuck in.
cs_canallum_n6_h: A guided tour in one take
cs_canallum_n5_b: The room you are in is captured in 360°, so the polished floor, the steel and the mirror reflect that room. Dusty sunbeams come in through each opening, trimmed by frames, eaves and trees. Dirt at the foot of the walls and stains on the concrete and the marès are drawn in the shader, with no new textures. Clouds catch the sunset, the walk focuses on what you look at, and a button path-traces the current view into a photo.

cs_review_tagline: The AI grades, the teacher signs off.
cs_review_intro: A beta app for grading university assignments with AI, built with a teacher who was already grading with ChatGPT. That meant ZIPs and spreadsheets going back and forth every round, checking each paper and its report in separate files, and explaining the same corrections to the chat again and again. Here the activity's materials go in once, Claude grades the whole batch against the rubric, the teacher validates each grade in one viewer, and every correction becomes an example for the rest.
cs_review_n1_b: Each activity keeps its brief, rubric, reference solution and grading guide, so nothing is uploaded or explained twice. For every rubric item the AI's value stays next to the teacher's, and the app exports the grade sheet the campus takes and the spreadsheet the teacher already used.
cs_review_n2_h: The model judges, the code scores
cs_review_n2_b: Claude Opus reads each submission against the rubric and decides, item by item, whether it meets the rubric, with a quote and a page for every deduction. Each quote is checked against the PDF, and the grade is worked out in code with exact fractions: the model never picks points. Claude also drafts the rubric from the grading guide, for the teacher to confirm.
cs_review_n3_b: Word, ODT or PDF, every submission goes through a document service in a container — LibreOffice to convert, PyMuPDF to strike out the student's name and ID — before Claude sees it, and the teacher can open exactly what the AI read. The data stays in the EU, on a self-hosted Supabase.
cs_review_n4_h: A batch that survives a deploy
cs_review_n4_b: Vercel Workflow runs the batch one submission per step: the first on its own, to warm the prompt cache, then five at a time. After a failure or a deploy halfway through, it picks up where it left off, without paying for any grading twice. The web app and the document service ship together as one Vercel project.
cs_review_n5_b: The viewer puts the rubric, the work and the report side by side, with every deduction underlined on the page. The rest came from what the teacher asked for: settling a contested item across the whole batch at once, seeing which rubric items many students miss, and knowing how often the AI agrees.

cs_lacasaestudio_tagline: From WordPress to a site that takes requests.
cs_lacasaestudio_intro: The website of La Casa Estudio, a recording project based at producer Youth's residential studio in Albuñuelas, Granada. In 2026 it moved from WordPress to Astro, with an admin for everything the studio changes often. Then it started asking for changes on Telegram, and an agent makes them.
cs_lacasaestudio_n1_h: Off WordPress without losing a link
cs_lacasaestudio_n1_b: Astro 7 on Vercel: the public pages ship almost no JavaScript, the home page is rendered on the server and cached for a minute, and everything is in Spanish and English. Content and photos moved into a self-hosted Supabase, and the old WordPress addresses, media files included, redirect with a 301 to their new home. A floating Spotify player sits on every page, and the studio's Instagram on the home page.
cs_lacasaestudio_n2_h: An admin the studio runs itself
cs_lacasaestudio_n2_b: Backline, past work, photos and the site's texts are edited at /admin: Google sign-in for a list of editors, row-level security on every write, a Tiptap editor for the texts and drag and drop to reorder. Each text comes in both languages, with a button that translates it into the other; Claude does it in GitHub Actions without blocking the admin, and the text lands on its own.
cs_lacasaestudio_n3_b: A Telegram bot turns each message into a comment on that chat's GitHub issue. A Claude coordinator that can only read reads the conversation and the work in progress and decides what each message is: a new change, another round on one in progress, an approval or a question. It asks one thing at a time until it knows what changes, where and how it should end up, and starts nothing new without a yes.
cs_lacasaestudio_n4_b: Claude Code makes the change in GitHub Actions, on its own branch, and its code only touches how the public site looks and reads: a check fails any of its branches that touches config, dependencies, migrations, auth or the admin. The preview link comes back to the chat, writing «publicar» puts it on the web (the code checks for that word, not the model) and the chat gets word when it is live. Texts stored in the database go another way: the chat changes them one allow-listed field at a time, shows each change first and can undo it.
